new.n: Alamo Club, 3 miles south of Tomahawk on Hwy 51 (1940)
new.pl: Old US 51, about 3 miles south of Tomahawk, Lincoln County
new.st: A 1940 newspaper ad places the Alamo Club, with dining and dancing, "3 miles South of Tomahawk On Highway 51" (Merrill Daily Herald, 1 Mar 1940, p. 8). The pin is a placeholder 3 miles south of town; the roadside lot on the old 51 alignment still has to be found. Pin set 3 road miles from downtown along US 51 as the 1950 USGS topo draws it (the pre-freeway line, south-east toward Road Lake), so it sits near the Road Lake end of the old highway; good to about 500 m.
new.t: Roadhouse yards, parking areas and the ground by the door collect coins and tokens. Find the old 51 alignment on the 1938 aerial. Private land: ask.
src: Merrill Daily Herald, 1 Mar 1940, p. 8, ads (newspapers.com image 1123137646)
new.pinev: 3.0 road miles from downtown Tomahawk along US 51 as drawn on the 1950 USGS Tomahawk 1:48,000 topo

new.n: Daniel Shaw Lumber Co. Flambeau Farm and company store (1870s-1900s)
new.pl: Flambeau-Chippewa confluence, by the old Flambeau post office (sec. 34 T33N R7W), Rusk County
new.v: Company-store tokens, coins, harness and farm iron
new.st: The Daniel Shaw Lumber Co.'s 900-acre supply farm stood 'sixty miles up the Chippewa River from Eau Claire ... at the confluence of the Flambeau River and the main stream', with about $10,000 of buildings and a company general store. A rival store opened at the nearby Flambeau post office in the early 1880s. Shaw's second camp (C. A. Bullen's, 56 miles from Eau Claire) was at the same confluence. The farm was offered for $35,000 in 1906 and still unsold in 1909 (manager C. S. Newell). Pin: the confluence as NHDPlus draws it, beside the Flambeau P.O. on the 1901-05 plat; the farm's 900 acres spread around it, and the Holcombe Flowage (1950) now covers the low ground, so the farmyard has to be found on the 1880s plat and the 1938 aerials.
new.t: Look for the farmyard and store on high ground by the confluence: company-store tokens, harness and farm iron, the root cellar. Private land: ask.
src: Reynolds, The Daniel Shaw Lumber Company (1957), archive.org danielshawlumber00reyn (PC read) pp 47-50, 54
https://archive.org/details/danielshawlumber00reyn

new.n: Shaw logging camp between the Flambeau and Deer Tail Creek (1870s-80s)
new.pl: Midway between the Flambeau River and Deer Tail Creek, about 6 miles above their mouths, Rusk County
new.st: A Daniel Shaw Lumber Co. camp stood 'midway between the Flambeau River and Deer Tail Creek', six miles above their mouths (1870s-80s). Shaw and Elias Moses built two large dams on Deer Tail Creek in 1879 (see the sec. 17 T34N R5W and Stitt dam pins). Pin: the midpoint between the points 6 river miles up each stream from its mouth on the Chippewa, measured on NHDPlus lines; the two points are 7 km apart, so this is good only to about 3.5 km.
new.t: Logging camps leave a clearing, cellar holes and a dump. Check LiDAR around the pin for the clearing. Private or county land: ask.

new.n: Daniel Shaw Lumber Co. boarding house, Shawtown (to 1900)
new.pl: Shawtown, by the Shaw mill at the south outlet of Half Moon Lake, Eau Claire
new.st: The Daniel Shaw Lumber Co. ran a boarding house at Shawtown (keeper James McDonald), abandoned by 1900, near the mill at the south outlet of Half Moon Lake. Pin: beside the Shaw mill pin; the 1880s Eau Claire Sanborn maps should show the building.
new.t: Boarding-house yards shed coins, tokens and buttons. City land: ask Eau Claire Parks; private lots: ask.

pfaff-shawtown-shingle-mill.st: Reynolds (1957): Shaw's original mill stood 'at the south outlet of Half Moon Lake ... Shawtown or West Eau Claire' and was rebuilt on the same spot after the 1867 fire. The company also had a hose house (p 88) and used the Crescent Mills gristmill in Eau Claire (p 49).

pfaff-half-moon-canal.st: Reynolds (1957): there were two Half Moon Lake canals, a quarter-mile upper canal from the Chippewa and a shorter lower canal, with mills at the mouth of the lower one. The Half Moon Lake Canal Co. was chartered in 1859, with a wing dam and boom.

set.n: Chautauqua Point grounds (later Presbyterian camp), Lake Chetek
set.pl: Wooded point on the north side of Lake Chetek, just east of town, Barron County
set.pinev: Best-fit wooded point on Lake Chetek proper (1951 and 1978 USGS topos)

pfaff-pokegama-chautauqua.st: By July 1922, "the grounds at Chetek, formerly known as Chautauqua point", a 13-acre tract, belonged to the Chippewa Presbytery. More than 1,000 people came to each meeting of its summer conference (Eau Claire Leader, 9 Jul 1922, p. 4). A 1908 postcard titled "Chautauqua Grounds, Chetek, Wis." shows tents among the trees (Wisconsin Historical Society). A Presbyterian camp or conference ground on the Chetek chain on a 1930s-60s map would mark the spot. In 1914 the Wisconsin Sunday School Association, which ran a training camp "at Chetek Lake", hoped to buy the "Chautauqua grounds at Chetek" (Eau Claire Leader, 7 Jul 1914, p. 4). The site was still the "Presbyterian camp ground, Chetek" in 1939 (Chippewa Herald-Telegram, 20 Apr 1939, p. 4). It is not the same place as the Chetek Baptist Assembly Grounds of the 1940s. In 1915 a two-week YMCA boys' camp, with tents, boats and a diving tower, was "located at Chautauqua Point on Lake Chetek" (Eau Claire Leader, 22 Jul 1915, p. 8). The pin sits on Pokegama Lake, north of The Narrows. Lake Chetek proper lies south of The Narrows, so unless the writer meant the whole chain, the point was probably on Lake Chetek itself and not on Pokegama Island. Pin moved from Pokegama Island to the best fit on Lake Chetek itself: the wooded point that juts south into the lake just east of town (secs. 20/29). On the 1951 and 1978 USGS topos it is the only unbuilt, wooded point of about the right size (roughly 13-15 acres) on Lake Chetek proper, and it is the nearest point to the town landing. No map labels it, so this is a best fit, good to about 800 m. Pfaff's "Pokegama Island" (the island in Pokegama Lake, north of The Narrows) stays the other candidate. The "Bible Camp" in sec. 18 on the 1951 topo is on the upper chain, not Lake Chetek, and is likely the 1940s Baptist grounds.
